The name sounds grand, the solutions look like magic, and the fear is that you either remember the trick or you do not. entry.title: The Problem with AI Memory Across Different Tools
entry.summary: I use ChatGPT, Claude Code, and local AI models regularly. Each tool serves a different purpose, but they all share one limitation: the context accumulated in one tool rarely follows me to another. This means repeating explanations, reconstructing previous decisions, and losing valuable context when switching between tools. I've started exploring how Obsidian, Markdown files, and MCP integrations can help create a shared knowledge source accessible to different AI assistants. The approach is promising, but challenges remain around retrieving relevant information, keeping it updated, and capturing new knowledge reliably. In my latest article, I share my experience, the limitations I've encountered, and the approach I'm experimenting with. Read the full article: When AI Memory Doesn't Follow You Between Tools How are you managing persistent memory across multiple AI tools?

Under the Bank Secrecy Act, financial institutions must file reports of cash transactions exceeding $10,000 (daily aggregate amount), according to FinCEN. entry.title: Aegis — The Privacy-First AI DevSecOps Side Hustle Powered by Local Open-Source AI
entry.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Team Submission: Krish (@krishtrue)
Keshav (@Ikeshav26) Every developer and freelancer knows the feeling: you run a security audit before handing off a project to a client, and suddenly your terminal floods with dozens of alerts — leaked API keys, outdated CVEs, SQL injection risks, and unescaped inputs. Triaging and manually writing code patches for all of them takes hours of tedious context switching. Large enterprises spend thousands of dollars on tools like Snyk or GitHub Advanced Security. But for freelancers, boutique development agencies, and solo founders, existing solutions present two massive roadblocks: The Privacy & Compliance Dilemma: You cannot feed confidential client code or unpatched zero-day vulnerabilities into closed cloud AI APIs (like OpenAI or Anthropic). Doing so violates NDAs, enterprise security policies, and client trust. The Per-Token Margin Killer: Closed AI APIs charge per token. Analyzing whole files and generating diffs for hundreds of security alerts across dozens of repos destroys the economics of a security side hustle. Aegis is a privacy-first, automated DevSecOps platform and security remediation bot with open-source AI at its very core. It connects to your GitHub repositories via a GitHub App, triggers asynchronous security scans (Semgrep for static analysis, Gitleaks for secrets, Trivy for dependencies), and uses local open-source AI models via Ollama optimized with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to automatically generate surgical code fixes and open pull requests directly on GitHub.

Semgrep / Gitleaks / Trivy] C --> D[Local Ollama Engine
Open-Weight Coding LLM + DPO] D --> E[Automated GitHub PR
Patch + AI Code Review]

entry.title: Keeping sensitive source encrypted on disk while still running Python code
entry.summary:
AI coding tools need to read project files. Some source code should still stay out of the workspace in plaintext. I built AILatch for that boundary: files stay encrypted on disk, while Python code can run with plaintext materialized only inside the AILatch process. The basic flow is: pip install ailatch
ailatch lock secret.py cat secret.py # ordinary file reads see ciphertext ailatch run secret.py # run the program without restoring plaintext
ailatch run decrypts the entry file in memory and keeps the working-tree file encrypted. Encrypted Python modules can still import each other, and application code can use normal open() and pathlib reads through the runtime hooks. When I need to inspect or edit a locked file, AILatch provides a controlled plaintext view: ailatch open . ailatch show secret.py
The project also includes encrypted backups and recovery commands: ailatch lock secret.py --recovery ailatch restore secret.py ailatch recover secret.py
This is aimed at filesystem-level reads by AI tools and ordinary file utilities. It does not claim to stop a privileged local attacker who can inspect process memory or persuade a user to decrypt a file. Stronger isolation still requires operating-system permissions, process isolation, and careful credential handling. AILatch currently targets Python 3.11+ and is primarily tested on Windows and macOS. Repository and full command reference: github.com/lo2589/AILatch Tags: #opensource #python #security #ai
